questions.q: How is database corruption a fundamentally different problem from the fragmentation and stale statistics covered earlier in this chapter?
options: Corruption means a page on disk doesn't match what SQL Server expects — a correctness problem that can silently hand a wrong result to your application, not just a performance problem that makes queries slower
Corruption is simply a more severe form of fragmentation and is fixed the same way, with ALTER INDEX REBUILD
Corruption only affects statistics, never actual table data
There is no real difference — all three are performance issues fixed by the same maintenance commands
questions.explain: Fragmentation and stale statistics still return correct answers, just slower or with a worse plan. Corruption can silently break correctness itself.

questions.q: What does DBCC CHECKDB actually validate?
options: The physical and logical integrity of every object in the database — page checksums, allocation consistency, and b-tree structure
Only whether SQL Server Agent jobs completed successfully
Only whether statistics are up to date
Only whether indexes are fragmented above 30%
questions.explain: CHECKDB is a comprehensive integrity check across the whole database's physical and logical structure, distinct from performance-tuning commands.

questions.q: Why should restoring from a known-good backup almost always come before running DBCC CHECKDB with REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS?
options: Because REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS can permanently delete corrupted rows, pages, or allocation units to make the database consistent again — consistent, not complete — while a backup actually gives the real data back
Because REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS is faster than restoring from backup in every case
Because backups cannot be restored while a database is corrupted
Because REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS never actually removes any data
questions.explain: Repair trades an unknown amount of permanently missing data for a database that stops erroring; a backup restores the actual data.

questions.q: How does Azure SQL Database/Managed Instance handle database integrity checking differently than SQL Server on an Azure VM, per this lesson?
options: On Azure SQL Database/Managed Instance, Microsoft runs integrity checks as part of the managed service; on an Azure VM (IaaS), scheduling DBCC CHECKDB is still the DBA's own responsibility, same as on-prem
Azure SQL Database requires the DBA to manually run CHECKDB nightly, while Managed Instance and VMs never need it
Integrity checking is identical across all three Azure SQL deployment options with no platform difference
None of the Azure SQL deployment options support any form of integrity checking
questions.explain: The PaaS options (Azure SQL Database, Managed Instance) are managed by Microsoft for this; the VM option is IaaS, so it's the DBA's own job.

questions.q: What does WITH NO_INFOMSGS accomplish when running DBCC CHECKDB?
options: It suppresses routine object-count informational messages so real errors don't get lost in the noise
It permanently deletes corrupted data automatically
It runs CHECKDB without reading any pages from disk
It forces the database into single-user mode
questions.explain: NO_INFOMSGS is purely about output clarity — it doesn't change what CHECKDB checks or repairs.
